results.question: What does the document say about methods?
results.answer: The document states that the request method token is the primary source of request semantics, indicating the purpose of the request and what the client expects as a successful result [p.72]. Method semantics can be further specialized by certain header fields when those don't conflict with the method [p.73]. The method token is case-sensitive, and standardized methods are by convention defined in all-uppercase US-ASCII letters [p.73]. Standardized methods are not resource-specific, since uniform interfaces provide better visibility and reuse, and a standardized method ought to have the same semantics when applied to any resource [p.73]. The spec defines standardized methods including GET, HEAD, and POST [p.73]. All general-purpose servers MUST support GET and HEAD, while all other methods are OPTIONAL [p.74]. An origin server receiving an unrecognized or unimplemented method SHOULD respond 501 (Not Implemented), and one receiving a recognized but disallowed method SHOULD respond 405 (Method Not Allowed) [p.74]. Additional methods outside the spec ought to be registered in the HTTP Method Registry [p.74]. Standardized methods are generic, potentially applicable to any resource [p.155]. Definitions of new methods cannot change the parsing algorithm or prohibit content on request or response messages [p.155].

results.question: What does the document say about methods?
results.answer: The document says the request method token is the primary source of request semantics, indicating the purpose of the request and what the client expects as a successful result [p.72]. A method's semantics might be further specialized by header fields if those don't conflict with the method [p.72][p.73]. The method token is case-sensitive because it might be used as a gateway to object-based systems with case-sensitive method names, and by convention standardized methods are defined in all-uppercase US-ASCII letters [p.73]. Standardized request methods are not resource-specific, since uniform interfaces provide better visibility and reuse in network-based systems, and once defined a standardized method ought to have the same semantics when applied to any resource, though each resource determines whether those semantics are implemented or allowed [p.73]. The specification defines GET (transfer a current representation of the target resource), HEAD (same as GET but do not transfer the response content), and POST (perform resource-specific processing) [p.73]. All general-purpose servers MUST support GET and HEAD; all other methods are OPTIONAL [p.74]. The set of methods allowed by a target resource can be listed in an Allow header field, though it can change dynamically [p.74]. An origin server receiving an unrecognized or unimplemented method SHOULD respond with 501 (Not Implemented), and one receiving a recognized and implemented method not allowed for the target resource SHOULD respond with 405 (Method Not Allowed) [p.74]. Additional methods outside the specification's scope ought to be registered in the "Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Method Registry" [p.74]. Standardized methods are generic and potentially applicable to any resource, so new methods are preferably registered in a document not specific to a single application or data format [p.155]. Since message parsing needs to be independent of method semantics (aside from responses to HEAD), definitions of new methods cannot change the parsing algorithm or prohibit content on either the request or response message [p.155]. Definitions of new methods can specify that only zero-length content is allowed by requiring a Content-Length header field with a value of "0", and new methods cannot use the special host:port and asterisk forms of request target allowed for CONNECT and OPTIONS, respectively; a full URI in absolute form is needed [p.155].
